content: Ascorbic acid injection is a vitamin approved by the FDA for the treatment of scurvy. Common adverse reactions include injection site reactions such as pain and swelling, diarrhea, iron overload, and nephrolithiasis (kidney stones). For adults, ascorbic acid is recommended for the prevention and treatment of scurvy. Parenteral administration (via injection) is preferred for patients with acute ascorbic acid deficiency or for those with uncertain absorption of orally ingested ascorbic acid. Symptoms of mild deficiency may include improper bone and tooth development, gingivitis, bleeding gums, and loose teeth. Conditions such as febrile states, chronic illnesses, and infections (e.g., pneumonia, whooping cough, tuberculosis, diphtheria, sinusitis, rheumatic fever) increase the need for ascorbic acid. Hemovascular disorders, burns, delayed fracture healing, and wound healing also necessitate an increased daily intake. Ascorbic acid is typically administered orally. However, when oral administration is not feasible or malabsorption is suspected, it can be given intramuscularly, intravenously, or subcutaneously. Intramuscular administration is the preferred parenteral route due to better utilization of the vitamin. For intravenous injection, dilution in a large volume of parenteral solution, such as normal saline or glucose, is recommended to minimize adverse reactions. The average protective dose for adults is 70 to 150 mg daily. In cases of scurvy, doses of 300 mg to 1 gram daily are recommended, with up to 6 grams administered parenterally in normal adults without evidence of toxicity. For wound healing, doses of 300 to 500 mg daily for 7 to 10 days, both preoperatively and postoperatively, are generally sufficient, though larger amounts may be recommended. For severe burns, daily doses of 1 to 2 grams are advised. In other conditions requiring increased ascorbic acid, three to five times the daily optimal allowance may be adequate. Pressure may develop within the vial during storage. Care should be taken when withdrawing the solution, and pressure should be relieved by inserting a sterile empty syringe into the vial to equilibrate pressure. When using dispensing vials, aseptic technique is essential. The entire contents should be dispensed in aliquots under a laminar flow hood without delay or within 4 hours after entry. Any remaining content should be discarded after the first withdrawal. Stoppers should be prepared with a suitable antiseptic solution. The solution should not be used unless it is clear and the seal is intact. Parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration. There is limited information regarding off-label guideline-supported use of ascorbic acid injection in adults. Non-guideline-supported uses include adjunct therapy for iron supplementation and treatment of AIDS virus infection associated with pregnancy. For pediatric patients, there is limited information regarding FDA-labeled or off-label use of ascorbic acid injection. Similarly, there is no FDA guidance on its use in geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or patients with renal or hepatic impairment. There is also no guidance on its use in immunocompromised patients. Ascorbic acid injection is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA, meaning animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and it is unknown whether it can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. It should only be administered to pregnant women if clearly needed. There is no Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) guidance on its use in pregnant women. Caution is advised when administering ascorbic acid injection to nursing mothers. Transient mild soreness may occur at the site of intramuscular or subcutaneous injection. Rapid intravenous administration may cause temporary faintness or dizziness. Diabetics, patients prone to recurrent kidney stones, those undergoing stool occult blood tests, and individuals on sodium-restricted diets or anticoagulant therapy should avoid excessive doses of ascorbic acid over extended periods. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is a water-soluble vitamin that appears as a white or slightly yellow crystal or powder with a light acidic taste. It is an antiscorbutic agent. Upon exposure to air and light, it gradually darkens. In its dry state, it is reasonably stable in air, but in solution, it rapidly oxidizes. It is freely soluble in water, sparingly soluble in alcohol, and insoluble in chloroform, ether, and benzene. The chemical name is L-ascorbic acid. In humans, an exogenous source of ascorbic acid is required for collagen formation and tissue repair. Ascorbic acid is reversibly oxidized to dehydroascorbic acid in the body, and both forms are believed to play a role in oxidation-reduction reactions. The vitamin is involved in tyrosine metabolism, conversion of folic acid to folinic acid, carbohydrate metabolism, synthesis of lipids and proteins, iron metabolism, resistance to infections, and cellular respiration. Deficiency of ascorbic acid results in scurvy, primarily affecting collagenous structures, with lesions developing in bones and blood vessels. Administration of ascorbic acid completely reverses the symptoms of deficiency. Ascorbic acid injection is available as a clear, colorless to slightly yellow sterile solution for intravenous, intramuscular, or subcutaneous use. It contains no preservatives and should be stored between 2°C to 8°C (36°F to 46°F) and protected from light. The solution should remain in its carton until the time of use.
